result: HP1α binds uniformly along DNA molecules, incorporating into both compacted and uncompacted regions at similar rates, demonstrating that compacted DNA remains accessible to HP1α from solution.
evaluation: Claims C8-C12 are supported by DNA curtain experiments with fluorescently labeled HP1α (Figure 1E-L). The data show uniform binding along DNA and comparable incorporation rates into compacted versus uncompacted regions, with quantitative measurements at different HP1α concentrations. The conclusion that compacted DNA remains accessible (C12) logically follows from the experimental observations.

result: HP1α compacts DNA at a rapid rate (47 kbp/s at 50 μM) by capitalizing on DNA fluctuations that bring distal segments together, with compaction initiating at the untethered DNA end where lower tension allows more conformational flexibility.
evaluation: Claim C13 provides quantitative data from DNA curtain experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). Claims C14 and C15 are mechanistic interpretations supported by polymer physics principles and citations to relevant literature. The model is consistent with the observed localization of compaction initiation and rapid compaction rates.

result: HP1α remains soluble up to 400 μM in 70 mM KCl without DNA but readily forms phase-separated condensates in the presence of DNA with a critical HP1α concentration of ~50 μM that is largely invariant of DNA concentration.
evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are supported by the phase diagram in Figure 2A showing condensate formation patterns. The critical concentration determination (C18) and the observation of continuous size reduction rather than sharp transitions with varying DNA concentration (C19-C20) are directly demonstrated. The persistence of condensates even at extreme HP1α:DNA ratios (C21) is shown in supplementary data.

result: The apparent dissociation constant for HP1α-DNA interactions ranges from 0.3 to 10 μM, and condensate size scales with both HP1α and DNA concentration according to a power law relationship.
evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by anisotropy data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) and citation to prior work. Claim C23 is demonstrated by power law fits to condensate size data in Figure 2C. Both claims are quantitatively supported with appropriate statistical analysis.

result: HP1α can undergo LLPS without DNA at 40 mM KCl (~400 μM), but at 75 mM KCl the critical concentration exceeds 800 μM.
evaluation: Claim C24 is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C. Claim C25 is supported by citation to prior work (Larson et al., 2017). The salt-dependence of HP1α phase separation is clearly demonstrated.

result: Increasing DNA length from 147 bp to 2.7 kbp decreases the critical HP1α concentration for LLPS from 50 μM to 3 μM, but further increases to 9 kbp show no additional decrease. DNA compaction occurs at concentrations as low as 500 nM but at significantly reduced rates.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by phase diagrams comparing different DNA lengths (Figure 2A,E). Claims C28-C29 are supported by DNA curtain data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C) showing compaction at low concentrations with quantitative rate measurements. The non-linear relationship between compaction rate and concentration (C29) suggests additional complexity beyond simple binding kinetics.

result: HP1α-DNA condensate coalescence time increases dramatically with DNA length: 147 bp DNA condensates coalesce rapidly, 2.7 kbp DNA requires >100-fold longer, and 9 kbp DNA condensates cannot complete coalescence within an hour.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are directly supported by time-lapse imaging in Figure 2D showing coalescence behavior for different DNA lengths. The dramatic increase in coalescence time with DNA length is clearly demonstrated and quantified.

result: HP1α recovery after photobleaching is unaffected by DNA length, with t1/2 values of ~2 s across DNA lengths from 147 bp to 50 kbp, matching in vivo measurements.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by FRAP experiments in Figure 3A-C showing consistent recovery rates across DNA lengths. Claim C35 compares these rates to published in vivo data with appropriate citations. The consistency across DNA lengths and agreement with in vivo data strongly support these claims.

result: HP1α rapidly exchanges within and between condensates (seconds timescale), while DNA remains segregated in long-lived (>1 hr) sub-condensate domains after fusion.
evaluation: Claim C36 is a conclusion supported by FRAP and mixing experiments. Claim C37 is demonstrated by two-color HP1α mixing experiments (Figure 3D). Claim C38 is shown by two-color DNA mixing experiments (Figure 3E). The contrasting dynamics of HP1α versus DNA are clearly demonstrated.

result: DNA recovery rates in condensates are proportional to DNA length, and MNase digestion of DNA results in rapid coalescence and mixing of previously segregated DNA domains.
evaluation: Claim C39 is supported by YOYO-1 FRAP experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C). Claim C40 is demonstrated by MNase treatment experiments (Figure 3F). These results provide strong evidence that DNA polymer properties determine its mobility within condensates.

result: HP1α-compacted DNA domains (~10 kbp) resist forces up to 40 pN, with smaller structures rupturing at 5-20 pN, indicating size-dependent stability. The energetic barrier is ~1 kbT/bp of compacted DNA.
evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by optical trapping force-extension measurements (Figure 4C-D). Claim C43 is an interpretation of the size-dependent rupture data. Claim C44 is calculated from the area between force-extension curves. The quantitative measurements and calculations support these claims.

result: Successive stretch-relax cycles result in progressively more DNA being stably sequestered by HP1α, suggesting that strain induces polymer rearrangements or force-dependent selection of binding interactions.
evaluation: Claim C45 is directly observed in optical trapping experiments (Figure 4C). Claim C46 is a mechanistic interpretation of this observation. While the exact mechanism remains speculative, the observation of increased compaction after strain is clearly demonstrated.

result: At low forces, HP1α-DNA condensates compact over time even without free HP1α in solution, while at sustained high forces they disassemble at rates independent of free HP1α concentration.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by optical trapping experiments with waiting periods (Figure 4E-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E). The force-dependent behavior and independence from free protein concentration during disassembly are clearly demonstrated.

result: The hinge domain of HP1α is sufficient for both DNA compaction and condensate formation, compacting DNA twice as fast as full-length HP1α and forming condensates at a 4-fold lower critical concentration (12.5 μM vs 50 μM).
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by DNA curtain experiments (Figure 5B-C) showing compaction by the hinge domain alone. Claims C53-C54 are supported by phase separation assays (Figure 5D-E) comparing critical concentrations. The enhanced activity of the isolated hinge domain is clearly demonstrated.

result: The NTE promotes HP1α activity (deletion reduces compaction ~20-fold and abolishes condensate formation with short DNA), while the CTE inhibits activity (deletion decreases critical concentration 10-fold and increases compaction rate 3-fold).
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by phase separation assays (Figure 6A-B) and DNA curtain experiments (Figure 6C-E) with deletion mutants. Claim C59 is a conclusion logically derived from the deletion experiments. The opposing regulatory roles of NTE and CTE are clearly demonstrated.

result: HP1β compacts DNA slowly but stably, HP1γ compacts faster than HP1β but rapidly disassembles when free protein is removed, and neither achieves the rapid compaction rates of HP1α.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by DNA curtain experiments comparing the three paralogs (Figure 7C-E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C). The differential compaction kinetics and stability are clearly demonstrated through direct comparison.

result: HP1γ forms condensates with 3 kbp DNA at higher critical concentrations than HP1α and does not form condensates with 147 bp DNA, while HP1β does not form condensates regardless of DNA length.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by phase separation assays (Figure 7F-G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) comparing condensate formation by the three paralogs with different DNA lengths. The differential phase separation capabilities are clearly demonstrated.

result: The HP1α hinge domain is both necessary and sufficient for condensate formation in the context of HP1 paralogs. Swapping the HP1α hinge into HP1β or HP1γ enables condensate formation at even lower critical concentrations than HP1α (2-fold and 10-fold lower, respectively).
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by phase separation assays with hinge swap mutants (Figure 7H-I). Claims C68, C70, and C72 are conclusions logically derived from the experimental observations. The domain swap experiments clearly demonstrate the critical role of the hinge domain and its enhanced activity outside its native context.

result: HP1β and HP1γ inhibit HP1α condensate formation when premixed, but when added to pre-formed HP1α condensates, HP1β invades and dissolves them while HP1γ enriches in them without destabilization.
evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by competition assays (Figure 8A). Claims C74-C75 are supported by experiments adding paralogs to pre-formed condensates (Figure 8B-C). The differential effects of HP1β versus HP1γ on pre-formed condensates are clearly demonstrated.

result: Background: Mammalian heterochromatin forms stable domains despite rapid HP1 exchange (seconds), and these domains can be rapidly disassembled in response to cellular cues.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C76-C78 are background knowledge supported by citations to prior work. These establish the biological context and paradox that motivates the study.

result: Background: The three HP1 paralogs have distinct biological roles, with HP1α associated with repression, HP1β with both activation and repression, and HP1γ with transcription promotion. HP1 proteins bind DNA/chromatin with weak affinity and induce condensation.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are background knowledge supported by citations to prior work. These establish the known properties of HP1 paralogs that inform the study design.

result: Background: HP1α undergoes LLPS in vitro when phosphorylated and with DNA, and Drosophila HP1a forms phase-separated condensates in vivo. HP1β cannot undergo LLPS with DNA alone but can be recruited to chromatin phases. Recent work questions whether HP1 heterochromatin exhibits liquid-like behavior in cells.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 are background knowledge supported by citations to prior work. These establish the current understanding and controversies regarding HP1 phase separation.

result: Background: HP1α contains a chromodomain (binds H3K9me), chromoshadow domain (mediates dimerization), hinge domain (binds DNA), and N/C-terminal extensions (regulate oligomerization). The hinge domain is essential for heterochromatin localization in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are background knowledge about HP1α domain structure and function, supported by citations to prior work. These establish the structural framework for the domain deletion and swap experiments.
